solution.concept_anchor: Alauddin Husain 'Jahan-suz' — Ghurid defeat of Ghaznavids at Ghazni (1150 CE)
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is the strong distractor because Muhammad of Ghor is the most famous Ghurid ruler associated with Indian campaigns, and students may assume he was also the one who defeated the Ghaznavids — not recognising that an earlier Ghurid ruler, Alauddin Husain, destroyed Ghazni in 1150.
elimination_logic: Recall: The Ghurid destruction of Ghazni occurred in 1150 CE — before Muhammad of Ghor's campaigns in India (1192 onward); eliminate (b) Muhammad of Ghor.
Recall: 'Jahan-suz' means World-Burner — an epithet given for burning Ghazni; this is associated with Alauddin Husain specifically.
Eliminate (a) Mahmud of Ghazni — he was a Ghaznavid ruler, not a Ghurid; he could not have destroyed his own dynasty's base.
Eliminate (c) Muizzuddin Bahram Shah — a later Delhi Sultanate figure, not connected to the Ghurid-Ghaznavid conflict.
Retain (d): Alauddin Husain, known as 'Jahan-suz,' destroyed Ghazni in 1150 CE.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes Muhammad of Ghor — the most famous Ghurid ruler — for Alauddin Husain 'Jahan-suz' who actually sacked Ghazni. Students associate the Ghurids' rise primarily with Muhammad of Ghor's Indian campaigns and forget that an earlier Ghurid ruler was responsible for the decisive defeat of the Ghaznavids at their own capital.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ghurid displacement of the Ghaznavids as the dominant power in Afghanistan is the essential precondition for understanding why the Ghurids then expanded into India.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Mahmud of Ghazni was the founder of Ghaznavid power — he could not have sacked his own capital.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Muhammad of Ghor's campaigns began in the 1170s–1190s — the sack of Ghazni in 1150 CE predates his rise to prominence. He consolidated Ghurid power in India after Ghazni had already fallen to an earlier Ghurid ruler.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Muizzuddin Bahram Shah was a mid-13th century Delhi Sultan — entirely unrelated to the Ghurid-Ghaznavid conflict.
• Option (d) — Correct: Alauddin Husain earned the epithet 'Jahan-suz' (World-Burner) for his systematic burning of Ghazni in 1150 CE, in revenge for the Ghaznavids killing members of his family. This act established Ghurid supremacy in the region.

Value Addition:
• The burning of Ghazni (1150 CE) was motivated partly by revenge — the Ghaznavids had killed two of Alauddin Husain's brothers.
• After Ghazni's fall, the Ghaznavid remnant retreated to Lahore, making Punjab the last Ghaznavid territory — which the Ghurids then absorbed in 1186 CE.
• The fall of Ghazni redirected Ghurid ambition eastward — toward the Indian subcontinent.

solution.concept_anchor: Moinuddin Chishti — arrival in Ajmer circa 1192, followed conquest
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) attributes 17 invasions to Muhammad of Ghor rather than Mahmud of Ghazni — students who know '17' is the traditional number but are uncertain which ruler it applies to will choose (a).
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): 17 invasions is the traditional count associated with Mahmud of Ghazni, not Muhammad of Ghor — (a) is incorrectly matched.

Evaluate (b): Moinuddin Chishti arriving in Ajmer before the Ghurid conquest contradicts the historical pattern — Sufi settlement followed, not preceded, military conquest; (b) is incorrectly matched.
Evaluate (c): Alauddin Husain 'Jahan-suz' earning his epithet from burning Ghazni is historically correct — this pair is correctly matched.
Evaluate (d): The Tabaqat-i-Nasiri was composed by Minhaj-us-Siraj, not Hasan Nizami — Hasan Nizami wrote the Taj-ul-Maasir; (d) is incorrectly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) exploits a reversed-causation trap: students who know Moinuddin Chishti is associated with the Ghurid conquest period may assume he preceded it as a missionary advance. In fact, his settlement in Ajmer (c. 1192) followed the Second Battle of Tarain — Sufi settlement patterns followed military security. Option (a) exploits the '17 invasions' as an easily misattributed detail.
solution.final_explanation:
Identifying correctly matched pairs requires precise attribution — the standard UPSC test of whether a student knows the specific entity behind a general fact.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: The traditional count of approximately 17 invasions applies to Mahmud of Ghazni, not Muhammad of Ghor. Muhammad of Ghor conducted far fewer campaigns — his India strategy was quality over quantity.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Moinuddin Chishti's arrival in Ajmer (c. 1192 CE) coincided with the Ghurid conquest — it followed military events, not preceded them. There was no Sufi 'advance party' preparing populations for conquest.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: Alauddin Husain earned the epithet 'Jahan-suz' (World-Burner) specifically for burning Ghazni in 1150 CE, avenging his brothers' deaths at Ghaznavid hands.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Taj-ul-Maasir was written by Hasan Nizami, not Minhaj-us-Siraj. Minhaj-us-Siraj wrote the Tabaqat-i-Nasiri.

Value Addition:
• The '17 invasions' figure for Mahmud of Ghazni is itself a historiographical debate — some scholars count differently based on what qualifies as a separate 'invasion.'
• Moinuddin Chishti's dargah in Ajmer remains one of the most visited Sufi shrines in South Asia.
• Hasan Nizami's Taj-ul-Maasir is particularly valuable for accounts of Qutbuddin Aibak's military campaigns.

solution.concept_anchor: Rajput internal rivalry — Prithviraj–Jaichandra conflict weakening unified resistance

statement_analysis.statement: Prithviraj III of the Chahamana (Chauhan) dynasty controlled Delhi (Dhillika) and Ajmer — territories that would later become the geographic core of the Delhi Sultanate.
statement_analysis.reason: Prithviraj III's domains included Delhi (Dhillika) and Ajmer — both of which became central to early Sultanate administration. Aibak used Delhi as his base, and the Sultanate's very name derived from control of this city.

statement_analysis.statement: The internal conflict between Prithviraj III and Jaichandra of the Gahadavala dynasty weakened the possibility of a united Rajput response to Ghurid invasion, as the two most powerful Rajput rulers were rivals rather than allies.
statement_analysis.reason: The Chahamana–Gahadavala rivalry is historically documented — Prithviraj and Jaichandra were not allies, and this internal division meant that when the Ghurids attacked in 1191 and 1192, there was no unified Rajput coalition comparable to the one assembled against Mahmud at Waihind.

statement_analysis.statement: Prithviraj III was captured by Muhammad of Ghor at the Battle of Chandawar (1194 CE), after which he was taken to Ghazni.
statement_analysis.reason: Prithviraj III was captured at the Second Battle of Tarain (1192 CE), not at Chandawar. Chandawar (1194 CE) was fought against Jaichandra of the Gahadavala dynasty. This is one of the most commonly tested battle-ruler confusions.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is the strong distractor because Statements 1 and 2 are both correct and clearly stated, leading students to assume Statement 3 is also correct without carefully checking which battle involved Prithviraj's capture.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Prithviraj's control over Delhi and Ajmer is historically established — correct.
Verify Statement 2: The Chahamana–Gahadavala rivalry and its impact on unified Rajput resistance is historically recognised — correct.
Challenge Statement 3: Prithviraj was captured at Tarain II (1192), not Chandawar (1194). Chandawar was fought against Jaichandra. Statement 3 conflates two different battles and rulers — incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 correct — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 3 uses a real event (Prithviraj's capture) but attributes it to the wrong battle. Both Tarain II and Chandawar are Ghurid victories of the same period, making the substitution feel plausible. Students who remember 'Prithviraj was captured by Muhammad of Ghor' but don't remember which battle may mark Statement 3 correct. The specific battle (Tarain II, 1192) is what separates informed from superficially prepared students.
solution.final_explanation:
The political context of Rajput resistance to Ghurid invasion involves both geographic and political dimensions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Prithviraj III controlled Delhi (Dhillika) and Ajmer — the geographic heartland of what would become the Delhi Sultanate. When Aibak took these territories, he inherited the administrative infrastructure of an existing power centre.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Chahamana–Gahadavala rivalry was a significant internal division. Prithviraj and Jaichandra were rivals — the story of Jaichandra's daughter Sanyogita's abduction by Prithviraj (from the Raso) captures this enmity, though its historicity is disputed.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Prithviraj III was captured at the Second Battle of Tarain (1192 CE). Chandawar (1194 CE) was the battle in which Jaichandra was defeated. This is the classic UPSC confusion between two consecutive Ghurid victories.

Value Addition:
• Delhi's strategic importance — controlling routes between Punjab and the Gangetic plain — made it the natural capital for any north Indian empire.
• The Chahamana dynasty is also called the Chauhan dynasty — Prithviraj III is the most famous ruler of this Rajput clan.
• After Tarain II, Aibak used Delhi as his administrative base, effectively transferring political power from the Chahamanas to the Ghurids.

solution.concept_anchor: Muhammad of Ghor — assassinated at Dhamyak on the Indus
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) places the assassination at Lahore, which students may associate with Muhammad of Ghor and Qutbuddin Aibak's administrative base — making it a plausible-sounding geographic substitute for the actual location.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Lahore was Aibak's administrative base — not the location of Muhammad's assassination; geographic swap.
Eliminate (b): Ghazni was the Ghurid capital — Muhammad was not assassinated there; another geographic swap.
Eliminate (d): Tarain was the location of the 1191 and 1192 battles — not Muhammad's assassination site; temporal-geographic confusion.
Retain (c): Dhamyak on the Indus is the historically recorded location of Muhammad of Ghor's assassination in 1206 CE.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap substitutes Lahore — the most frequently mentioned city in the context of late Ghurid administration — for Dhamyak on the Indus, the actual assassination site. Students who associate Muhammad of Ghor with Punjab (through Tarain and Lahore) but haven't memorised the specific assassination location will default to Lahore as the answer.
solution.final_explanation:
The circumstances and location of Muhammad of Ghor's assassination are precise factual details that UPSC has tested.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Lahore was the administrative capital of Qutbuddin Aibak's Indian territories — not where Muhammad of Ghor was killed.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Ghazni was the Ghurid dynasty's original capital in Afghanistan — Muhammad was not assassinated there.
• Option (c) — Correct: Muhammad of Ghor was assassinated at Dhamyak, a location on the Indus river, in 1206 CE. The assassins were either Khokhars (a local tribe who had previously rebelled) or Ismaili agents — historians debate this.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Tarain is associated with the 1191 and 1192 battles — it has no connection to Muhammad's assassination.

Value Addition:
• Muhammad of Ghor had no direct male heirs — this is why his death triggered a division of the empire among his Mamluk commanders.
• The Khokhars were a tribal group of the Punjab region who had been subdued by Muhammad but remained resentful — making them plausible suspects.
• 1206 CE is the conventional founding date of the Delhi Sultanate precisely because Muhammad's assassination removed the central Ghurid authority that Aibak had served under.

solution.concept_anchor: Ghurid succession — correct sequence from Tarain II to Sultanate founding
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places Muhammad of Ghor's assassination before the Battle of Chandawar, which would be historically impossible since Chandawar was fought in his name — students uncertain about exact dates may accept this reversal.
elimination_logic: Anchor: Second Battle of Tarain (1192) must come first — this is the decisive military event opening the Gangetic plain.
Battle of Chandawar (1194) follows Tarain II — Jaichandra is defeated after Prithviraj's defeat; this sequence is fixed.
Muhammad of Ghor's assassination (1206) must come after both battles — he was alive during both campaigns.

Qutbuddin Aibak's assumption of the sultanate (1206) follows immediately after the assassination — the correct sequence is Tarain II → Chandawar → Muhammad's assassination → Aibak's sultanate, matching option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap in option (c) reverses Muhammad's assassination and Chandawar — placing the assassination before the battle. Students who know the approximate decade (1190s–1206) but not the precise sequence may accept this. The anchor is that Muhammad was alive and active until 1206 — all military campaigns in India during 1192–1206 were conducted in his name.
solution.final_explanation:
The chronological sequence of the Ghurid-to-Sultanate transition:

Correct sequence: Second Battle of Tarain (1192) → Battle of Chandawar (1194) → Muhammad of Ghor's assassination (1206) → Qutbuddin Aibak assumes sultanate (1206)

• Second Battle of Tarain (1192): The decisive military turning point — Prithviraj III defeated and captured. This opens the Gangetic plain to Ghurid expansion.
• Battle of Chandawar (1194): The destruction of the Gahadavala kingdom — Jaichandra defeated. Varanasi and the Doab come under Ghurid control.
• Muhammad of Ghor's assassination (1206): At Dhamyak on the Indus. All campaigns between 1192 and 1206 were conducted under his authority, so his death in 1206 is the post-terminus for those events.
• Qutbuddin Aibak assumes sultanate (1206): The formal founding of the Delhi Sultanate follows immediately upon Muhammad's death.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a) reverses Tarain II and Chandawar.
• Option (c) places the assassination before Chandawar — impossible since Muhammad was alive during Chandawar.
• Option (d) places Aibak's sultanate before Muhammad's assassination — logically impossible.

Value Addition:
• The year 1206 CE simultaneously marks Muhammad's assassination and Aibak's sultanate — both happened in the same year.
• Aibak's reign was brief (1206–1210 CE); his more organisationally significant successor was Iltutmish.
• The Battle of Chandawar is sometimes called the 'Battle of Etawah' in older scholarship — the location is near modern Firozabad.

solution.concept_anchor: Ghaznavid Punjab — entry route for Ghurids, not just Ghaznavid legacy
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strong distractor because both A and R are correct and thematically connected — students who correctly identify both as true may assume the causal relationship without examining whether Punjab's Ghaznavid administrative framework specifically enabled Ghurid entry.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? A states Punjab's Ghaznavid administrative establishment made it the natural entry route for Ghurid forces. This is correct — the Ghaznavids had created roads, administrative posts, and a Muslim-governed Punjab that the Ghurids used as their base for Indian operations.
Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? R states Malik Ayaz was appointed governor of Lahore by Mahmud and was the first Muslim administrator of Punjab. This is factually correct.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? R identifies Ayaz's appointment as the origin of Ghaznavid administrative presence in Punjab. A claims this presence made Punjab the Ghurid entry route. R's statement about Ayaz's appointment does provide the causal foundation for A — the administrative infrastructure created by Ayaz (and his successors) under Ghaznavid rule is precisely what made Punjab a functioning base for Ghurid operations. R does explain A.

A correct + R correct + R explains A → option (a). Wait — re-examine: Does Ayaz's appointment specifically explain that Punjab was the 'natural entry route' for the Ghurids? The administrative framework created under Ayaz persisted and made Punjab accessible — yes, this causal chain is valid. Correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question tests whether students can correctly assess a genuine causal relationship — the trap is reversed-causation in the wrong options. Option (b) suggests A and R are both correct but causally unconnected, tempting students who suspect the connection is too neat. But the causal chain is genuine: Ayaz's appointment created the administrative infrastructure → that infrastructure made Punjab a functional Muslim-governed territory → which made it the natural entry route for the Ghurids a century later. Students who over-apply skepticism about causal claims will select (b) incorrectly.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ghaznavid administrative presence in Punjab and its role in enabling Ghurid expansion are causally connected in a genuinely traceable way.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Punjab's century-long Ghaznavid administration (from Malik Ayaz onward) created roads, administrative posts, and a Muslim-governed territory that the Ghurids naturally used as their base and entry route for campaigns into the Gangetic plain.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Malik Ayaz was appointed governor of Lahore by Mahmud of Ghazni — he was the first Muslim administrator of Punjab, establishing the Ghaznavid administrative presence that lasted until 1186 CE when the Ghurids displaced the last Ghaznavid ruler of Punjab.
• Causal Relationship: R (Ayaz's appointment creating Ghaznavid administrative infrastructure) genuinely explains A (Punjab becoming the natural Ghurid entry route) — the administrative framework created by Ghaznavid governors made Punjab a functioning base rather than an unfamiliar conquest zone for the Ghurids.

Correct answer: (a) — Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• The Ghaznavid line in Punjab continued until 1186 CE — over 160 years of Muslim administration before the Ghurids replaced them.
• The Ghurids absorbed the Ghaznavid administrative personnel and infrastructure rather than starting from scratch — continuity, not disruption, characterised the transition.
• Lahore remained a major administrative centre through the Ghaznavid, Ghurid, and Sultanate periods — its importance predating all these dynasties.

solution.concept_anchor: Romila Thapar's historiography of Somnath — deconstruction of nationalist myth

statement_analysis.statement: Romila Thapar's historical work on Somnath argues that the 'myth' of Somnath as a definitive moment of Hindu–Muslim conflict is a later construction, drawing on the testimony of Persian court chronicles, Sanskrit inscriptions, and Jain sources that present divergent accounts of the event.
statement_analysis.reason: Thapar's 'Somnatha: The Many Voices of a History' uses multiple source types — Persian chronicles, Sanskrit temple inscriptions, and Jain texts — to show that contemporary Indian sources do not present Somnath as a singular civilisational wound; this retrospective framing was a 19th-century colonial and nationalist construction.

statement_analysis.statement: The absence of contemporaneous Indian-language accounts of Ghaznavid and Ghurid invasions means that historians are entirely dependent on Persian court chronicles, making objective historical reconstruction impossible.
statement_analysis.reason: While Indian-language contemporaneous chronicles are indeed largely absent, historians supplement Persian chronicles with Sanskrit inscriptions, temple records, Jain texts, numismatic evidence, and archaeological data — the situation is epistemologically challenging but not a complete bar to historical reconstruction.

statement_analysis.statement: K.A. Nizami and Irfan Habib represent distinct historiographical approaches to the Sultanate period — Nizami focused on institutional and religious history while Habib emphasised agrarian-economic structures and social history.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately characterises the major interpretive schools: Nizami's work on Sufism and institutional Islam under the Sultanate, and Habib's economic history focused on agrarian structures, exploitation, and the experience of peasant communities.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is the strong distractor because Statement 2 sounds authoritative and epistemologically nuanced — students may mark the 'entirely dependent' qualifier as acceptable given the real absence of Indian-language sources.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Thapar's multi-source methodology and her argument about the Somnath myth being a later construction is well-established in modern historiography — correct.

Challenge Statement 2: 'Entirely dependent' and 'impossible' are absolute claims — historians use inscriptions, numismatic evidence, and Jain texts alongside Persian chronicles; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: The Nizami–Habib disciplinary distinction is a recognised characterisation of the major modern interpretive schools — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 takes a genuinely accurate observation (absence of contemporaneous Indian-language chronicles) and extends it to an absolute conclusion ('entirely dependent,' 'impossible'). Students who know about the source problem may accept the full statement without questioning the absolutism of 'entirely' and 'impossible' — two qualifiers that historians would never use given the availability of inscriptions, coins, and Jain texts.
solution.final_explanation:
Historiographical literacy — knowing not just what happened but how we know it and what its interpretive limits are — is an increasingly tested UPSC dimension.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Thapar's work on Somnath demonstrated that the 'attack on Hindu civilisation' framing was primarily a 19th-century British colonial and later nationalist construction. Contemporary Indian sources — Sanskrit inscriptions, Jain texts — treat the event very differently from later nationalist accounts.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: While Indian-language contemporaneous chronicles are largely absent, this does not make reconstruction 'impossible' or historians 'entirely dependent' on Persian chronicles. Sanskrit inscriptions, numismatic records, Jain texts, and archaeological evidence supplement the Persian sources.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Nizami's work centred on institutional and religious history (Sufism, Ulema, Islamic administration) while Habib's focused on agrarian structures, economic exploitation, and social history — two genuinely different approaches.

Value Addition:
• Thapar, Habib, and Nizami represent three major pillars of modern Delhi Sultanate historiography — their methodological differences reflect broader debates in historical studies.
• Persian chronicles' panegyric bias means they exaggerate victories and omit defeats — cross-referencing with inscriptions is essential.
• Sanskrit prasastis (eulogistic inscriptions) occasionally mention Muslim raids as part of a ruler's military challenges — providing a rare Indian-perspective data point.

solution.concept_anchor: Slave dynasty nomenclature — Mamluk vs. Ilbari Turks distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strong distractor because 'Slave dynasty' is the universally used popular term — students may not know its historiographical critique and will choose the most familiar label.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): 'Slave dynasty' is a popular but historiographically imprecise term — modern historians prefer 'Mamluk' or more specifically 'Ilbari Turks' for the dynasty to which Aibak, Iltutmish, and Balban belonged.
Eliminate (b): 'Khilji dynasty' refers to Jalaluddin Khilji's successors — a later Sultanate dynasty; anachronistic here.
Eliminate (d): 'Shansabani dynasty' is the Ghurid ruling clan's name — Aibak was not a Shansabani; he was a Mamluk slave of the Ghurids.
Retain (c): 'Mamluk dynasty' or 'Ilbari Turks' is the more precise historiographical designation for the line beginning with Aibak.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap lies not in inventing a term but in making the popular term ('Slave dynasty') the distractor. Students who know Aibak founded the 'Slave dynasty' will choose (a) without knowing that modern historians prefer 'Mamluk' as a more precise term, and that 'Slave dynasty' is a later historiographical simplification that modern scholarship has critiqued.
solution.final_explanation:
The naming of Qutbuddin Aibak's dynasty is a historiographical question with practical UPSC implications.

• Option (a) — Less precise: 'Slave dynasty' is the traditional popular label, derived from the fact that Aibak, Iltutmish, and Balban were all originally slave-soldiers. However, modern historians critique this as an oversimplification — not all rulers in this line were slaves, and the term conflates different generations.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Khilji dynasty began with Jalaluddin Khilji in 1290 CE — a later and distinct Sultanate dynasty.
• Option (c) — Correct: 'Mamluk' (Arabic for 'owned') is the more precise historiographical term for the dynasty. 'Ilbari Turks' is even more specific — referring to the Central Asian Turkic lineage of Iltutmish and Balban's group within this dynasty.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 'Shansabani' refers to the Ghurid ruling family — Aibak was their Mamluk (slave-soldier), not a member of their ruling clan.

Value Addition:
• Not all rulers of the so-called 'Slave dynasty' were themselves slaves — Raziyya Sultan was Iltutmish's daughter, not a slave.
• The Mamluk institution — elite slave-soldiers who could rise to positions of power — was a common feature of Islamic polities from the 9th century onward.
• UPSC has previously tested whether students know that the 'Slave dynasty' is also called the 'Mamluk dynasty' — both labels appear in different textbooks.

Precise factual accuracy about the Somnath campaign and its aftermath is what this question tests.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 4 assigns Yildiz — a real Ghurid commander who actually inherited Ghazni — the role that belonged to Bakhtiyar Khilji in eastern India. Both are Ghurid Mamluk commanders of the post-1206 period, making the swap feel plausible. The specific geographic assignment (Yildiz = Ghazni/Afghanistan; Bakhtiyar Khilji = Bengal/Bihar; Qabacha = Sindh) is the precision knowledge this question tests.
solution.final_explanation:
Muhammad of Ghor's delegation model — distributing Indian administration among trusted Mamluk commanders — is the structural foundation of how the Delhi Sultanate emerged.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Aibak served as Muhammad's principal Indian viceroy, based at Lahore, coordinating all Ghurid Indian operations.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Bakhtiyar Khilji operated under Aibak's overall command, conducting the rapid small-cavalry raids into Bihar (c. 1200 CE) and Bengal (c. 1203–04 CE).
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Khwarazmian empire was expanding and threatening Ghurid western territories — Muhammad's divided attention made delegation to Mamluk commanders in India a strategic necessity.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Yildiz inherited Ghazni (Afghanistan) after Muhammad's assassination — he was never associated with Bengal or Bihar. Those territories were Bakhtiyar Khilji's domain under Aibak.

Value Addition:
• The three Mamluk successors to Muhammad of Ghor divided the empire: Aibak (India), Yildiz (Ghazni), Qabacha (Sindh/Multan).
• These three successors competed for dominance — Iltutmish defeated both Yildiz and Qabacha to become the undisputed Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate.
• The delegation model inadvertently created the Delhi Sultanate — when the central Ghurid authority (Muhammad) died, the delegates became independent rulers.

solution.final_explanation:
The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra are pivotal monuments for understanding the architectural transition at the Ghurid–Sultanate junction.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Both structures were initiated by Qutbuddin Aibak in the Ghurid period, c. 1192–93 CE — before the Delhi Sultanate's 1206 founding. This is a critical distinction: they are Ghurid-era buildings, not Delhi Sultanate-proper constructions.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Quwwat-ul-Islam was explicitly built using columns, brackets, and other elements from 27 demolished Hindu and Jain temples on the site. This material reuse is visually evident in the mosque today — the non-uniform columns of varying heights are the repurposed temple pillars.

Value Addition:
• The Quwwat-ul-Islam's name ('Might of Islam') reflects its symbolic function — demonstrating Ghurid power at the site of a former Rajput capital.
• The mosque's screen wall (added by Iltutmish) introduces true arches — contrasting with the corbelled construction of the original Aibak-era mosque, showing architectural evolution.
• Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra in Ajmer was built over a Sanskrit college — the name possibly derives from a fair (jhonpra = fair/gathering) held at the site for two and a half days.
